ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *swésōrder. Proto-Germanic *swestēr Proto-West Germanic *swester Old English sweostor Middle English suster English sister Inherited from Middle English suster, from Old English sweostor, from Proto-West Germanic *swester, from Proto-Germanic *swestēr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. Doublet of soror.

senses.d: A daughter of the same parents as another person; a female sibling.
ex: My sister is always driving me crazy.

senses.d: A female member of a religious order; especially one devoted to more active service; (informal) a nun.
ex: Michelle left behind her bank job and became a sister at the local convent.

senses.d: Any butterfly in the genus Adelpha, so named for the resemblance of the dark-colored wings to the black habit traditionally worn by nuns.
A senior or supervisory nurse, often in a hospital.
Any woman or girl with whom a bond is felt through the same biological sex, gender or common membership in a community, race, profession, religion, organization, or ism.
ex: Connie was very close to her friend Judy and considered her to be her sister.
Sisters are doing it for themselves / Standing on their own two feet
The short “naps” of the average Sister do not sway in the wind as that of a blonde.

senses.d: A form of address to a woman.
ex: "Listen, sister. I've got a job for you."

senses.d: A female fellow member of a religious community, church, trades union etc.
ex: Thank you, sister. I would like to thank the sister who just spoke.

senses.d: An entity that has a special or affectionate, non-hierarchical relationship with another.
A node in a data structure that shares its parent with another node.
To strengthen (a supporting beam) by fastening a second beam alongside it.
ex: I’m trying to correct my sagging floor by sistering the joists.

senses.d: To be sister to; to resemble closely.

a nun; a female member of a religious community

attributively: of an entity that has a special relationship with another

fr:sœur.gl: sister (a daughter of the same parents as another person; a female sibling)

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French soeur, from Old French suer (nominative), from Latin soror (cf. also the Old French oblique form seror from the Latin accusative sorōrem), from Proto-Italic *swezōr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
From Latin soror, from a diminutive form or based on the model of fratello. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *swezōr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
Inherited from Old Spanish ermana, from Latin germāna.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese irmãa, yrmãa, from Latin germāna (“sister”), from the adjective germānus (“of siblings”); more at irmão. By surface analysis, irmão + -a (forms feminine equivalents).
Inherited from Old French none, nominative singular of nonain, from Late Latin nonna. Compare German Nonne.
Inherited from Latin soror (nominative) via loss of /-r/ and then adjustment of /-o/ to the more typical (for feminine nouns) /-a/.

ety.text: Latin sororlbor. Portuguese soror Learned borrowing from Latin soror.
Inherited from Old Spanish ermano, from Vulgar Latin *germānus (“brother”), from Latin germānus (“of a brother or sister”). Compare English germane. Displaced Old Spanish fradre, from fratēr.
